probes_issued: Consider a multi-threaded web server running on a system with 64 GB of physical RAM. Thread A just finished processing a request and loaded a frequently used configuration page into physical RAM. Thread B, running on a different CPU core, has its TLB flushed due to a context switch. When Thread B now accesses that same configuration page's virtual address, the hardware TLB lookup returns a miss. The page is guaranteed to be sitting in physical RAM — it was placed there only microseconds ago by Thread A. In this situation, does the hardware need to involve the operating system kernel or initiate a disk read to fulfill this memory access, or is there something that can be resolved entirely within the hardware using data already present in main memory? What specifically does the hardware need to locate before it can conclude the page is truly absent from physical memory?

Consider this situation: A process has been running for several minutes, and all of its currently active pages are resident in physical RAM. The valid/present bit is set to 1 for every one of these pages in the page table. Now, a context switch occurs to a different process, and the new CPU core clears its TLB entirely. The original process is scheduled back in and attempts to access a memory address corresponding to one of those active pages. The page is definitely in RAM — no one has swapped it out. If the student's assumption is that a TLB miss always results in disk I/O, what would happen in this scenario? Would the system be forced to read from disk when the data is already sitting right there in physical memory, and if so, what would be the purpose of the page table stored in RAM?
